catalog_quote: Stress falls on one of the two first syllables of the phonological word. Primary stress is lexically determined and contrastive as shown in (5). (5) a. fáluma m-ábürühà-ny-on coconut neg-fall-prog-3.f 'the coconut is not falling' b. l-abûrü-ha-nya máysturu 3.m-write-distr-prog teacher 'the teacher is writing' However, stress is assigned according to different rules in nouns than in verbs. The examples in (5) show lexically determined stress which does not change at affixation. Nouns, on the other hand, may undergo stress shift when taking a possessive prefix according to a rule that a possessed noun should always carry stress on the second syllable regardless of its lexical stress. (6) a. lasúsu 'soup' b. ni-lásusu-n 1.sg-soup-poss 'my soup' c. muréy 'nance' d. nu-múrey 1.SG-nance 'my nance' e. gárada 'letter' f. ni-gárada-n 1.sg-letter-poss 'my letter' g. fáluma 'coconut' h. nu-fáluma 1.sg-coconut 'my coconut' ... As for secondary stress, it is much less predictable and I have yet to figure out which generalizations can be made regarding its distribution. [Sec. 7.6] Clitics in Garifuna are like affixes in that they never have primary stress, though they may have secondary stress. Secondary stress is not distinctive in the grammar but rather assigned according to regular metric rules (Taylor, 1955; Cayetano, 1992).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is confined to a two-syllable window at the left edge of the phonological word (initial or second syllable); within that window its position is lexical and contrastive (ábürüha 'fall' vs abǘrüha 'write'). Verb stems keep their lexical stress under affixation; a noun bearing a possessive prefix takes stress on the second syllable of the prefixed word whatever its lexical stress. Affixes and clitics never carry primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Written with a grave accent throughout the grammar; author says its distribution is 'much less predictable and I have yet to figure out which generalizations can be made' (p. 23), but in Sec. 7.6 states 'Secondary stress is not distinctive in the grammar but rather assigned according to regular metric rules (Taylor, 1955; Cayetano, 1992)'; passives receive secondary stress on the final syllable (Sec. on -wa passive).
new_statements.exceptions: Possessed nouns shift to second-syllable stress (lasúsu -> ni-lásusu-n); some particles/enclitics (irrealis lan, vocative enclitic, ga utterance-finally) carry their own stress; auxiliaries in imperatives variably stressed depending on verb-phrase length; Suazo (1991) reports initial- vs final-stress verb doublets ('pasivo' vs 'intensivo/enfático') which the author tentatively links to gendered speech (p. 97-98). JIPA 2023 (Abtahian et al., p. 394) independently: 'Although the placement of stress in Garifuna is usually predictable, it can be contrastive' with pairs /ˈariha/ 'doze' vs /aˈriha/ 'see', /ˈabɯrɯha/ 'fall' vs /aˈbɯrɯha/ 'write'.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (prefixes count: nu-múrey). Examples are drawn from elicited sentences and citation forms in a time-aligned corpus; Honduran variety (Triunfo de la Cruz, Tela). The JIPA acoustic figures are from connected speech (NWS passage) of a Belizean (Hopkins-area) speaker.
new_statements.identity_note: Haurholm-Larsen 2016 describes the Honduran variety (fieldwork in Triunfo de la Cruz, Tela, 2012-2015); the JIPA 2023 Illustration and Taylor 1955 describe Belizean Garifuna (Hopkins / Seine Bight). All are gari1256 (Glottolog lists no dialect-level codes used here). Older literature calls the language Black Carib / Central American Island Carib.

sources.quote: 2.22.61. Stress is not predictable, (cf. tanága her back, tágani her enemy); and the existence of such minimal pairs as áhamacá to fly versus ahámaca to pounce (upon) or to grab (at), and those cited under 1.1, is proof enough of its distinctive character. Nevertheless, the functional yield of this opposition is not great; and, as is the case with English ádult ~ adúlt, forms are to be found in whose pronunciation different speakers employ different accentuations. [...] 2.22.62. A large proportion (I cannot be more precise) of words having three or more syllables has stress on the second and on every third succeeding syllable thereafter, as in sabádu shoes, nisábadu my shoes, uarígabagába butterfly. It is not clear to me whether, in words containing two stresses, there is any difference between one and the other, and if so which is the stronger; except that stress before pause is always weaker, while a second and word-final stress is entirely lost in contexts where the following form is stressed on the first syllable. Words of two syllables are, for the most part, stressed on the first syllable; while monosyllabic words always carry stress when pronounced in isolation.

sources.note: 'Prosodic features' (p. 394-395): 'Although the placement of stress in Garifuna is usually predictable, it can be contrastive', with minimal pairs from Cayetano 1992 (/ˈariha/ 'to doze' vs /aˈriha/ 'to see'; /ˈabɯrɯha/ 'to drop; to fall' vs /aˈbɯrɯha/ 'to write'); does not state the default rule; instrumental: stressed vowels longer, higher f0 (242 vs 213 Hz) and intensity (72 vs 70 dB) in 64 words of the NWS passage; unstressed vowels reduce to schwa or devoice finally. Speaker from Hopkins/Seine Bight area, Belize.
